apps.readme:
# VS Code

A full VS Code in the browser, proxied behind the front door — Microsoft's own `code serve-web`,
the same CLI VS Code itself ships, pinned to one commit and sha256-verified before it ever runs.
No Rust, no binary checked into this repo: the CLI is fetched from Microsoft at first start.

This bundle carries three elements:

| kind | name | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| dashboard | `vscode` | the launcher: a tile on the Home grid at `vscode.adi` that starts the editor and opens it with its connection token |
| service | `vscode` | the hive service that fetches, verifies and runs `code serve-web`, at `vscode-server.adi` |
| project | VS Code | the project scaffold both are recommended to file under |

Install into a project of its own:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install <marketplace>/vscode --new-project "VS Code"
```

That lands all three. The service is copied live in the same act (it is **on-demand**: nothing
runs until the first visit — see "Launching it"); the launcher arrives archived, like every
dashboard, and is started with:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace start vscode        # the launcher's dashboard id, as `marketplace apps` lists it
```

or from its row on the Dashboards page. If you installed with `--no-start`, the service is started
by the launcher's first "Open", or by hand:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace start <marketplace>/vscode/services/vscode --project <id>
```

## Launching it

Once the launcher is started, VS Code is a tile on the Home grid of the control panel
(`app.adi`), the same as any other app on the machine. Opening the tile:

1. loads the launcher at `http://vscode.adi/`, which asks the control panel where the service
   stands — installed, copied live, answering;
2. if the editor is already running, hands you straight over to it; otherwise shows one button,
   **Open VS Code**, and says what opening it will do (a first start downloads the editor and
   accepts the licence below);
3. `/api/open` copies the service live if it is still parked, resolves the connection token the
   same way the service itself does (next section) — minting and writing one if there is none yet,
   so the first start serves with a token the launcher already knows — and answers a `302` to
   `http://vscode-server.adi/?tkn=<token>`;
4. the front door sees the visit, wakes the on-demand service, and holds the page ("Starting this
   service for you", reloading every two seconds) until the editor answers, then becomes it.

Through the mesh the same launcher at `vscode.<node>.n.adi` redirects to
`vscode-server.<node>.n.adi` — the one address for that node's editor that resolves from where the
viewer sits. `?stay` on the launcher's URL keeps it from handing a running editor over, for when
you want to read the page. `?folder=<path>` and `?workspace=<path>` are passed through to VS Code.

The launcher is two dependency-free Bun servers (`dashboards/vscode/frontend/index.ts`,
`dashboards/vscode/backend/index.ts`), the shape every dashboard has. The backend calls the control
panel's own API (`/api/marketplace`, `/api/hive`, `/api/marketplace/start-service`) server-side;
a page could not, since the panel refuses browser requests from other origins. It finds the panel
without relying on the `.adi` name, which a node without the resolver installed cannot use: the
panel's leased loopback port in the store's `ports/registry.json` first, then the front door by its
address (`ADI_FRONTDOOR_ADDR`) with `Host: app.<domain>`, then `http://app.<domain>` — or
`ADI_PANEL_URL` in the backend's environment to say outright. It needs the service installed **in
the same scope** (the same project, or both global): it finds the service through the install
ledger that landed it, and the token in the directory that install's service runs in.

**Moving from 0.2.0:** the service's host was `vscode.adi`; from 0.3.0 that is the launcher's, and
the service answers on `vscode-server.adi`. `adi-mono marketplace update <marketplace>/vscode
--project <id>` re-lands the service block with the new host (unless you edited it — then it is
left alone and said so, and the launcher would collide with it on `vscode.adi`), after which the
launcher can be installed: `adi-mono marketplace install <marketplace>/vscode/dashboards/vscode
--project <id>`.

## Licence terms — read before starting this

This service is a thin wrapper around Microsoft's own `code` CLI, which it downloads directly
from Microsoft (`update.code.visualstudio.com`) the first time it starts. **Nothing of Microsoft's
is redistributed by this bundle** — the repository ships none of their binary, only the pinned
commit and sha256 digests the script checks the download against.

**Starting this service accepts the VS Code Server Licence Terms**
(https://aka.ms/vscode-server-license) on behalf of whoever starts it — `code serve-web` is
launched with `--accept-server-license-terms` on every start, which is what that flag is for.
Read the licence before the first start if that matters to you; this README cannot substitute
for it. In particular, the licence Microsoft publishes for the VS Code Server **permits running it
for your own use or your team's use, not hosting it as a service for third parties** — do not put
this behind a login wall and sell seats on it. The launcher says the same thing beside its button,
because pressing it is the act that starts the service.

**Telemetry is on by default**, the same as it is in Microsoft's own VS Code — `code serve-web`
phones home to Microsoft unless told not to. Disable it per-start by setting `VSCODE_TELEMETRY:
"off"` in the service's `environment.static` block in `.adi/hive.yaml` before starting (it adds
`--disable-telemetry` to the launch). This disables the *server's* telemetry; a user's own
settings inside the editor (e.g. an extension with its own phone-home) are theirs to manage from
inside the workbench.

## First start takes a minute

On first start the service downloads the one archive matching the host's OS and CPU — Linux
(x64/arm64), macOS (x64/arm64) or Windows (x64/arm64), six combinations in total — from
Microsoft's update server, checks it against the sha256 pinned in `services/vscode.yaml` for that
exact combination, and caches the extracted `code` (`code.exe` on Windows) under `.vscode-cli/` in
the directory the service runs from (the project's own directory, when installed into one, which
is also what the editor opens by default — see "The workspace folder" below). Every later start
reuses the cache and is instant. `code serve-web` itself then downloads the actual server component
for the pinned commit into `.vscode-cli/cli-data/` (via `--cli-data-dir`, so that lands in this
service's own state rather than the host user's home directory) — also cached after the first
start.

The CLI version is pinned by its exact 40-hex commit (`--commit-id` on the `serve-web` invocation),
the same commit the six archives are downloaded for — a start never floats to whatever Microsoft
currently calls "latest stable".

The service declares no `start:` policy, so the hive's default for a proxied service applies:
**on-demand**. It is woken by a visit to its host and stopped again after sitting idle; the
launcher's redirect is such a visit.

## The connection token

`code serve-web` refuses every request without a connection token. On each start the script:

1. tries `adi-mono secrets read VSCODE_TOKEN` (**global** scope — a hive service has no project
   context to look a project-scoped secret up against, unlike an agent);
2. failing that, reuses whatever token it generated on a previous start, from
   `.vscode-cli/connection-token` (mode `0600`);
3. failing that (first start, no secret set), generates a random 32-byte token and writes it there.

The launcher resolves the token in the same order, and when neither the secret nor the file exists
it writes a fresh one to that file before redirecting — the service then reuses it (step 2), which
is what makes the very first open land in the editor rather than on a `403`.

Set the secret yourself to pick a token you already know, and to survive the state directory being
wiped:

```sh
adi-mono secrets set VSCODE_TOKEN   # value from stdin or --value
```

Whichever token is in force, the editor is at `http://vscode-server.adi/?tkn=<token>` — without
`?tkn=` (or with the wrong one) the server answers `403`. The launcher at `http://vscode.adi/` is
the way there that does not require knowing it.

## The workspace folder

`code serve-web --default-folder` sets what opens for a request that carries no `folder=` of its
own. This service passes it `$WORKSPACE_DIR`, which defaults to the directory the service itself
runs in — the project's directory, for a project-scoped install. Override it by setting
`WORKSPACE_DIR` in the service's `environment.static` block in `.adi/hive.yaml` before starting,
if you want it to open somewhere else — or open the launcher with `?folder=<path>` for one visit.

## Why no Rust, why no binary here

The upstream CLI is a prebuilt native binary — exactly the compiled shape a bundle may never carry
(`docs/marketplace-bundles.md`, "No Rust in an item"). So this bundle ships none of it: the
service's own script fetches the one matching archive by URL at **start** time, not at publish
time, and refuses to run anything whose sha256 doesn't match the digest pinned for that exact
platform/architecture in `services/vscode.yaml`. That script is itself the one named hole the same
document calls out — "a hive service's `runner.script` ... can `curl` a binary and execute it at
runtime" — stated plainly rather than papered over.

## How the bootstrap itself is written — one shell, two parsers

The installer lands the service as one file (`services/vscode.yaml`), so the whole bootstrap has to
be self-contained inside it. `runner.script.run` is handed to `sh -c` on Unix and to `cmd /C` on
Windows — one string, two completely different parsers. The run line here is kept to exactly one
thing neither parser can trip over:

```
bun -e "eval(process.env.VSCODE_BOOTSTRAP)"
```

No `$VAR` or `%VAR%` shell expansion, nothing from `% ^ & | < >` anywhere in that line — both `sh`
and `cmd` hand `bun` the one double-quoted argument intact. The actual bootstrap (the download,
the sha256 check, the extraction, the token handling, the `code serve-web` launch) is the
`VSCODE_BOOTSTRAP` value in `environment.static` just above it in the YAML: a plain environment
variable, injected straight into the child process's environment table by the Rust runner, which
never goes through either shell's parser at all — so it is free to contain anything, including the
very characters the run line itself has to avoid. `eval`, not `new Function`, is what picks it up:
a direct `eval()` keeps the enclosing module's scope (so `require`/dynamic `import` inside the
bootstrap work), where `new Function(...)` runs with no lexical scope at all.

**Windows walkthrough**, concretely: `cmd /C bun -e "eval(process.env.VSCODE_BOOTSTRAP)"` — `cmd`
sees one command (`bun`), two arguments (`-e` and the quoted string), and never interprets anything
inside the quotes because none of `cmd`'s own metacharacters (`% ^ & | < >`) appear there. `bun`
then reads `process.env.VSCODE_BOOTSTRAP` directly from its own process environment — not from
anything `cmd` expanded — and `eval`s it. Inside that bootstrap, Windows-specific branches use
`child_process.spawn`/`execFileSync` with an argument array (never a shell string), so the zip
extraction (`Expand-Archive` via `powershell.exe`) and the final `code.exe serve-web` launch are
never re-parsed by `cmd` either.

## Checking it works

```sh
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://vscode-server.adi/              # 403 — no token (once running)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://vscode-server.adi/?tkn=wrong"   # 403 — wrong token
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' "http://vscode-server.adi/?tkn=$TOKEN"  # 302 → the workbench
curl -s http://vscode.adi/api/status                                             # the launcher's view of the service
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{redirect_url}\n' http://vscode.adi/api/open   # 302 http://vscode-server.adi/?tkn=…
```

The launcher's own tests: `bun test dashboards/vscode/test`.

## Licence

MIT (this bundle). `code`/VS Code Server is Microsoft's own, under the VS Code Server Licence
Terms linked above — this bundle redistributes none of it.

apps.readme:
# 2048

The classic 2048, as one dashboard — a 4×4 sliding-tile puzzle with real slide/merge animations,
a best score that survives a reload, and nothing on the backend: every rule lives in the browser.

This bundle carries one element:

| kind | name | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| dashboard | `game-2048` | the game itself — frontend only, a one-route backend stub for the dashboard contract |

Install it:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install <marketplace>/game-2048
```

It arrives archived, same as every dashboard — start it from the Dashboards page, or:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace start <marketplace>/game-2048/dashboards/game-2048
```

Then open it by its hostname. No secret, no project, nothing else to configure.

## Why no backend logic

2048's entire rulebook — sliding, merging, spawning, win/lose detection — runs client-side; there
is nothing for a server to compute or to keep private. The backend half of this dashboard exists
only because the dashboard contract (`guides/dashboards.md`) needs one: it is the template's
own unmodified `backend/index.ts`, answering `/api/health` so the page's status dot has something
to poll, and nothing more. No route file was added.

## How it's built

`frontend/modules/game.ts` is the panel; `frontend/modules/.logic.ts` is the whole rulebook —
pure functions over a plain 4×4 number grid, no DOM, no randomness that isn't passed in as an
argument. The dot in its name keeps it off the shell's auto-mounted panel list (`guides/
dashboards.md`'s module discovery lists every `modules/*.ts` that doesn't start with `.`); the
panel reaches it at runtime as a same-origin `./.logic.js` import, which the frontend server
resolves straight back to this file.

The rules:

- **merge once per move**: scanned left-to-right (or the equivalent for the direction moved), a
  tile that has already merged this move never merges again — `[2,2,2,0]` slides to `[4,2,0,0]`,
  not `[4,4,0,0]`; `[2,2,2,2]` merges as two separate pairs, `[4,4,0,0]`.
- **spawn**: after every move that actually changes the board, one new tile lands on a random
  empty cell — 2 nine times out of ten, 4 the rest.
- **win**: reaching 2048 offers *Keep going* as well as *New game* — the board keeps playing, and
  nothing about reaching 2048 a second time re-fires the banner.
- **game over**: every one of the four directions is checked against the current board; only when
  none of them would change anything is it actually over, not merely "no empty cell left" (a full
  board that can still merge is not over).

`frontend/modules/game.ts` renders this onto a board of real DOM tiles kept alive across moves —
a tile that slides keeps its element and just gets new `--x`/`--y` custom properties (a CSS
`transition` on `left`/`top` does the sliding); a tile consumed by a merge is removed once the
slide finishes and a freshly minted tile appears at the destination with a short "pop" animation;
a spawned tile gets a "scale in" animation. The board is drawn as CSS percentages off one `SIZE`
constant, so it holds together at any panel width, and the same palette is used in light and dark
(the template's own ADI tokens already cover both — see `[data-theme="light"]` in `frontend/
index.html`).

Input: `ArrowLeft/Right/Up/Down` and `a`/`d`/`w`/`s` (case-insensitive, ignored while any text
input or textarea elsewhere on the page has focus), plus a touch swipe (24px minimum, whichever
axis moved further wins ties). Best score is `localStorage["adi.game2048.best"]`, scoped to the
browser, not the backend — there is nothing server-side to lose it with.

## Checking it works

```sh
bun test test/game-logic.test.ts
```

19 checks against `frontend/modules/.logic.ts` directly — no DOM, no server: every merge shape
(`mergeLine`), all four directions (`move`), the spawn distribution with an injected `rng`
(`addRandomTile`, `randomTileValue`), and game-over detection against both a mid-game and a
fully-deadlocked board (`isGameOver`).

A second, optional check covers what the logic tests structurally can't: whether the win/game-over
overlay is actually invisible when it should be. `.g2048__overlay` sets `display: flex` (to centre
its card), and an author stylesheet rule always outranks the UA's own `[hidden] { display: none }`
at equal specificity — so a missing `.g2048__overlay[hidden]` override renders the overlay (and
its "New game" button) permanently, over the board, regardless of the `hidden` attribute. Neither
`bun:test`'s DOM nor happy-dom compute CSS cascade, so this needs a real browser:

```sh
bun add -d playwright && bunx playwright install chromium   # one-time, not needed to play the game
bun test test/overlay-visibility.test.ts
```

It skips (with a warning, not a failure) if Playwright isn't installed — the dashboard itself has
no dependency on it.

## Licence

MIT.

apps.readme:
# Mines

A classic Minesweeper, as one dashboard — three standard difficulties, a guaranteed-safe first
click, chording, flags, a timer with a best time per difficulty kept in localStorage, and nothing
on the backend: every rule lives in the browser.

This bundle carries one element:

| kind | name | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| dashboard | `game-mines` | the game itself — frontend only, a one-route backend stub for the dashboard contract |

Install it:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install <marketplace>/game-mines
```

It arrives archived, same as every dashboard — start it from the Dashboards page, or:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace start <marketplace>/game-mines/dashboards/game-mines
```

Then open it by its hostname. No secret, no project, nothing else to configure.

## Why no backend logic

Mines' entire rulebook — mine placement, flood fill, chording, win/lose detection — runs
client-side; there is nothing for a server to compute or to keep private. The backend half of
this dashboard exists only because the dashboard contract (`guides/dashboards.md`) needs one: it
is the template's own unmodified `backend/index.ts`, answering `/api/health` so the page's status
dot has something to poll, and nothing more. No route file was added.

## How it's built

`frontend/modules/game.ts` is the panel; `frontend/modules/.logic.ts` is the whole rulebook —
pure functions over a plain grid of booleans and counts, no DOM, no randomness that isn't passed
in as an argument. The dot in its name keeps it off the shell's auto-mounted panel list
(`guides/dashboards.md`'s module discovery lists every `modules/*.ts` that doesn't start with
`.`); the panel reaches it at runtime as a same-origin `./.logic.js` import, which the frontend
server resolves straight back to this file.

The rules:

- **first click is always safe**: mines aren't placed until the very first reveal, seeded off
  that click — the clicked cell and its whole eight-neighbour ring are excluded from mine
  placement, so the opening move always clears real space instead of risking a 1x1 island.
- **flood fill**: revealing a cell with zero mine-neighbours cascades outward through every
  connected zero cell, stopping at (but still revealing) the first ring of numbered cells around
  each pocket. A mine is never pushed onto the flood — only an explicit reveal of its own cell can
  uncover one.
- **chording**: clicking an already-revealed number whose flagged-neighbour count matches its own
  value reveals every other neighbour at once — the standard "I trust my flags" shortcut. A
  mismatched count is a no-op; a wrongly-flagged neighbour that turns out to be a mine still loses,
  exactly as an ordinary click on it would.
- **win**: every safe cell revealed, independent of whether every mine got flagged. **Lose**:
  any mine revealed — the board then reveals every mine and marks any wrongly-placed flag.

Three difficulties, same as the original: Beginner (9×9, 10 mines), Intermediate (16×16, 40
mines), Expert (30×16, 99 mines) — escalating both board size and mine density for a real
difficulty curve.

`frontend/modules/game.ts` renders this onto a DOM grid sized off one `--cell-size` CSS variable,
recomputed on resize so Expert's 30 columns fit (and scroll, inside `.mines__viewport`) on a
375px phone exactly as they do on a desktop. The same flat palette (the template's own ADI tokens)
covers light and dark.

Input: left-click/tap a hidden cell to reveal it, a revealed number to chord it; right-click or a
~450ms long-press (cancelled by a 10px finger move, so a scroll never flags) to flag a hidden
cell. Arrow keys move a visible keyboard cursor, Space/Enter reveals or chords it, `F` flags it.
Pause blurs the board and stops the clock without resetting it. Best time is
`localStorage["adi.gamemines.best.<difficulty>"]`, scoped to the browser, not the backend — there
is nothing server-side to lose it with.

## Checking it works

```sh
bun test test/mines-logic.test.ts
```

14 checks against `frontend/modules/.logic.ts` directly — no DOM, no server: the safe-first-click
guarantee (`placeMines`, `reveal`), flood fill cascading and stopping at flags
(`reveal`/`floodReveal`), chording on a matched, mismatched, and wrongly-flagged neighbour set
(`chord`), and win/lose detection either cell-by-cell or in one cascading click.

A second, optional check covers what the logic tests structurally can't: whether the win/lose
overlay is actually invisible when it should be. `.mines__overlay` sets `display: flex` (to centre
its card), and an author stylesheet rule always outranks the UA's own `[hidden] { display: none }`
at equal specificity — so a missing `.mines__overlay[hidden]` override renders the overlay (and
its "New game" button) permanently, over the board, regardless of the `hidden` attribute. Neither
`bun:test`'s DOM nor happy-dom compute CSS cascade, so this needs a real browser:

```sh
bun add -d playwright && bunx playwright install chromium   # one-time, not needed to play the game
bun test test/overlay-visibility.test.ts
```

It skips (with a warning, not a failure) if Playwright isn't installed — the dashboard itself has
no dependency on it.

apps.readme:
# Blockfall

A falling-blocks puzzle, as one dashboard — a 10×20 well, the standard seven tetromino shapes
drawn from a 7-bag randomizer, SRS-style rotation with wall kicks, ghost piece, hold, a next-3
preview, soft/hard drop, DAS/ARR key repeat, lock delay, and a level curve that speeds gravity up
as you clear lines. Nothing on the backend: every rule lives in the browser, and the best score
survives a reload in `localStorage`.

This bundle carries one element:

| kind | name | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| dashboard | `game-blockfall` | the game itself — frontend only, a one-route backend stub for the dashboard contract |

Install it:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install <marketplace>/game-blockfall
```

It arrives archived, same as every dashboard — start it from the Dashboards page, or:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace start <marketplace>/game-blockfall/dashboards/game-blockfall
```

Then open it by its hostname. No secret, no project, nothing else to configure.

## Why no backend logic

Blockfall's entire rulebook — spawning, movement, rotation and wall kicks, collision, locking,
line clears, scoring and the level curve — runs client-side; there is nothing for a server to
compute or to keep private. The backend half of this dashboard exists only because the dashboard
contract (`guides/dashboards.md`) needs one: it is the template's own unmodified
`backend/index.ts`, answering `/api/health` so the page's status dot has something to poll, and
nothing more. No route file was added.

## How it's built

`frontend/modules/game.ts` is the panel — rendering, timing, input and persistence. The whole
rulebook lives in `frontend/modules/.logic.ts`: pure functions over a plain `Board` (a ROWS×COLS
grid of cell types) and a `Piece` (type, rotation state, and the board position of its own
bounding box), with no DOM and no randomness that isn't passed in as an injectable `rng`. The dot
in its name keeps it off the shell's auto-mounted panel list (`guides/dashboards.md`'s module
discovery lists every `modules/*.ts` that doesn't start with `.`); the panel reaches it at runtime
as a same-origin `./.logic.js` import, which the frontend server resolves straight back to this
file.

The rules:

- **7-bag randomizer**: `shuffledBag` returns one Fisher-Yates shuffle of all seven piece types;
  `PieceQueue` always keeps a full bag ahead of what's been drawn, so a `peek(3)` preview is never
  waiting on a shuffle that hasn't happened yet, and no piece is ever more than twelve draws away
  from its last appearance.
- **SRS rotation with wall kicks**: each piece's four rotation states are the standard SRS offset
  tables; `tryRotate` tries the "no kick" placement first, then walks the matching 5-point kick
  table (JLSTZ or the I piece's own, wider one) until one offset doesn't collide, or returns
  `null` if none do. O is rotationally symmetric in every state this file gives it, so it always
  "succeeds" with no kick and no shape change.
- **ghost piece**: `dropPiece`/`dropDistance` compute where the active piece would land without
  moving it — the panel draws that as a translucent outline, and recomputes it on every move.
- **lock delay**: a piece that becomes grounded doesn't lock immediately; `game.ts` starts a
  500ms timer the moment `isGrounded` turns true, cancels it if the piece moves off the ground
  again, and only locks when it actually elapses.
- **line clears, scoring, levels**: `clearLines` drops every full row and compacts the rest down,
  with fresh empty rows added at the top; `scoreForClear` is the classic 1/2/3/4-line table scaled
  by level; `levelForLines` advances one level per 10 lines; `gravityIntervalMs` shortens the fall
  interval each level, clamped so late levels stay playable instead of becoming an instant-drop
  wall.
- **hold**: swaps the active piece with the held one (or stashes it, if nothing was held yet),
  locked to once per piece so hold can't be chained into never losing control of the active piece.

Input: arrow keys to move/soft-drop (with DAS/ARR auto-repeat — an initial delay, then a faster
steady repeat, independently tuned for horizontal movement vs. soft drop), `↑`/`x` and `z` to
rotate clockwise/counter-clockwise, space to hard drop, `c` to hold, `p` to pause — all ignored
while any text input or textarea elsewhere on the page has focus. Touch gets its own button bar
(repeat-aware left/right/soft-drop, tap for rotate/hold/hard-drop) plus a swipe on the well itself
(a tap rotates, a swipe moves or hard-drops), shown below 640px width or on any coarse pointer.
Best score is `localStorage["adi.blockfall.best"]`, scoped to the browser, not the backend — there
is nothing server-side to lose it with.

## Checking it works

```sh
bun test test/game-logic.test.ts
```

27 checks against `frontend/modules/.logic.ts` directly — no DOM, no server: collision at every
boundary, move/ground/drop-distance, unobstructed rotation and every wall-kick path (including a
fully-blocked rotation returning `null`), O's trivial rotation, locking and line-clear mechanics
(a tetris, non-contiguous clears, nothing clearing), top-out detection, and the 7-bag (a shuffled
bag is always a permutation of all seven types, every consecutive run of seven draws is a full
set, and `peek` doesn't consume).

A second, optional check covers what the logic tests structurally can't: whether the pause/game-
over overlay is actually invisible when it should be. `.bf__overlay` sets `display: flex` (to
centre its card), and an author stylesheet rule always outranks the UA's own
`[hidden] { display: none }` at equal specificity — so a missing `.bf__overlay[hidden]` override
renders the overlay (and its "New game" button) permanently, over the board, regardless of the
`hidden` attribute. Neither `bun:test`'s DOM nor happy-dom compute CSS cascade, so this needs a
real browser:

```sh
bun add -d playwright && bunx playwright install chromium   # one-time, not needed to play the game
bun test test/overlay-visibility.test.ts
```

It skips (with a warning, not a failure) if Playwright isn't installed — the dashboard itself has
no dependency on it.

# Snake

A grid snake, as one dashboard — buffered turning so a fast corner never gets dropped or flips the
snake into itself, speed that ramps with length, an occasional bonus pickup that times out, a
Wall/Wrap mode toggle, pause, and a best score kept per mode. Nothing on the backend: every rule
lives in the browser.

This bundle carries one element:

| kind | name | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| dashboard | `game-snake` | the game itself — frontend only, a one-route backend stub for the dashboard contract |

Install it:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install <marketplace>/game-snake
```

It arrives archived, same as every dashboard — start it from the Dashboards page, or:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace start <marketplace>/game-snake/dashboards/game-snake
```

Then open it by its hostname. No secret, no project, nothing else to configure.

## Why no backend logic

Every rule — movement, collision, growth, pickups, scoring — runs client-side; there is nothing
for a server to compute or to keep private. The backend half of this dashboard exists only
because the dashboard contract (`guides/dashboards.md`) needs one: it is the template's own
unmodified `backend/index.ts`, answering `/api/health` so the page's status dot has something to
poll, and nothing more. No route file was added.

## How it's built

`frontend/modules/game.ts` is the panel; `frontend/modules/.logic.ts` is the whole rulebook — pure
functions over a plain grid, no DOM, no randomness that isn't passed in as an argument. The dot in
its name keeps it off the shell's auto-mounted panel list (`guides/dashboards.md`'s module
discovery lists every `modules/*.ts` that doesn't start with `.`); the panel reaches it at runtime
as a same-origin `./.logic.js` import, which the frontend server resolves straight back to this
file.

The rules:

- **movement**: a 20×20 grid. Each tick advances the head one cell in the current heading and
  drops the tail — unless the move eats something, in which case the tail stays and the snake is
  one cell longer.
- **input buffering**: up to two turns may queue ahead of the one being applied. A turn is only
  ever checked against the *last already-queued* direction (or the current heading, if the queue
  is empty), so a fast "down then left" to round a corner lands both turns in order — and a turn
  that would reverse into the snake's own neck is rejected at the moment it's queued, never
  silently applied two ticks later into a death that looks like a dropped input.
- **collision**: running the head into its own body is fatal. Running it into the cell the tail is
  about to vacate is **not** — the tail moves away the same tick, unless this move also grows the
  snake, in which case the tail stays and the same move is lethal.
- **wall vs wrap**: `wall` mode kills the snake against the board edge; `wrap` mode carries the
  head to the opposite edge instead. A segmented control at the top switches modes (starting a
  fresh game), and each mode keeps its own best score.
- **growth and scoring**: the regular pickup is worth 10 and always respawns somewhere the snake
  and the bonus (if one is live) aren't. Eating it has a chance of also spawning a bonus pickup
  worth 50, which disappears on its own after a fixed number of ticks if nobody gets to it.
- **difficulty curve**: tick speed ramps up with the snake's length (not with score or elapsed
  time), floored so a very long run stays controllable rather than becoming unplayable.
- **pause**: Space or P, or the on-screen Pause button — the overlay offers Resume as well as New
  game, and nothing ticks while it's up.

`frontend/modules/game.ts` renders this onto a board of real DOM elements kept alive across
ticks — every element is keyed by its *index* in the snake array rather than by a stable per-
segment id, which is what makes the whole body visibly crawl forward on a CSS `left`/`top`
transition with no special-casing: a non-growing move produces `[nextHead, ...snake.slice(0,
-1)]`, so index *i > 0*'s value after the move is exactly index *i - 1*'s value before it, and
just re-reading each index's new position off the updated array animates correctly. A growing move
only ever adds one element at index 0; nothing is removed mid-run. The bonus pickup draws its own
remaining-life as a shrinking ring. The board is drawn as CSS percentages off the `COLS`/`ROWS`
constants, so it holds together at any panel width, and the same palette is used in light and dark
(the template's own ADI tokens already cover both — see `[data-theme="light"]` in `frontend/
index.html`).

Input: `ArrowLeft/Right/Up/Down` and `a`/`d`/`w`/`s` (case-insensitive, ignored while any text
input or textarea elsewhere on the page has focus), a touch swipe (20px minimum, whichever axis
moved further wins ties), and Space/P for pause. Best score is
`localStorage["adi.gameSnake.best.<mode>"]`, one key per mode, scoped to the browser — there is
nothing server-side to lose it with.

## Checking it works

```sh
bun test test/game-logic.test.ts
```

31 checks against `frontend/modules/.logic.ts` directly — no DOM, no server: movement in all four
directions, wall-mode and self collision, the tail-vacate exception (and its growth-cancels-it
counterpart), wrap-mode edge wrapping, growth and scoring on both the regular and bonus pickup,
food/bonus never spawning on an occupied cell, the bonus pickup expiring on its own tick, the
length-based speed ramp, and the input queue — duplicate and reversing turns rejected at enqueue
time, the two-deep cap, and FIFO order on dequeue.

A second, optional check covers what the logic tests structurally can't: whether the pause/
game-over overlay is actually invisible when it should be. `.snake__overlay` sets `display: flex`
(to centre its card), and an author stylesheet rule always outranks the UA's own
`[hidden] { display: none }` at equal specificity — so a missing `.snake__overlay[hidden]`
override renders the overlay permanently, over the board, regardless of the `hidden` attribute.


apps.readme:
# Bricks

A brick-breaker, as one dashboard — a canvas-rendered paddle-and-ball game with hand-designed
levels, procedurally generated ones after that, multi-hit bricks, falling power-ups, lives, a
best score kept in localStorage, and frame-rate-independent physics with no tunnelling, even at
high ball speed.

This bundle carries one element:

| kind | name | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| dashboard | `game-bricks` | the game itself — frontend only, a one-route backend stub for the dashboard contract |

Install it:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace install <marketplace>/game-bricks
```

It arrives archived, same as every dashboard — start it from the Dashboards page, or:

```sh
adi-mono marketplace start <marketplace>/game-bricks/dashboards/game-bricks
```

Then open it by its hostname. No secret, no project, nothing else to configure.

## Why no backend logic

The whole rulebook — physics, collision, scoring, level progression — runs client-side; there is
nothing for a server to compute or to keep private. The backend half of this dashboard exists
only because the dashboard contract (`guides/dashboards.md`) needs one: it is the template's own
unmodified `backend/index.ts`, answering `/api/health` so the page's status dot has something to
poll, and nothing more. No route file was added.

## How it's built

`frontend/modules/.logic.ts` is the whole rulebook — pure functions over a plain coordinate
system (a fixed `WIDTH x HEIGHT` virtual board), no DOM, no canvas, no randomness that isn't
passed in as an argument. The dot in its name keeps it off the shell's auto-mounted panel list
(`guides/dashboards.md`'s module discovery lists every `modules/*.ts` that doesn't start with
`.`); `frontend/modules/game.ts` (the actual panel) reaches it at runtime as a same-origin
`./.logic.js` import, which the frontend server resolves straight back to this file.

The rules:

- **Paddle bounce angle depends on hit position.** Dead centre sends the ball straight up; the
  further toward an edge it lands, the more the ball is deflected toward that side, up to
  `MAX_BOUNCE_ANGLE` (62°) — speed is always preserved, so this redirects, never accelerates.
- **Collision is circle-vs-rectangle**, resolved by reflecting whichever axis (x or y) the ball
  penetrates *least* — the standard way to handle a corner hit without a special case for it.
- **No tunnelling, at any speed, on any frame.** Each ball's movement for a frame is split into
  enough substeps that no single substep can move it further than `MAX_SUBSTEP_DISTANCE` (90% of
  the smallest of the ball's radius, a brick's height, and the paddle's height) — so a ball fast
  enough to cross an entire brick in one naive frame-sized step is still caught mid-flight. This
  is frame-rate independent: a dropped frame (a big `dt`) just gets more substeps, not a skipped
  check.
- **Multi-hit bricks** take more than one hit to destroy, graded darker-to-brighter by remaining
  hit points so the damage is visible.
- **Levels**: the first three are hand-designed (`DESIGNED_LEVELS`); every level after that is
  procedurally generated, strictly harder as the level number grows — more rows (capped at 8),
  higher average hit points (capped at 4), and a higher fill density — via an injected `rng` so a
  given level is always reproducible in a test. A roll that would leave a layout entirely empty
  is forced to carry at least one brick, so every generated level is completable. Ball speed also
  increases per level (capped), the other half of the difficulty curve.
- **Power-ups** fall from a fraction of destroyed bricks (18%) and are caught by touching the
  paddle: **wide** (bigger paddle, 10s), **slow** (ball speed ×0.6, 8s), **multiball** (splits the
  current ball into extras, angled apart, capped at 6 balls total so it can't run away).
- **Lives**: starts at 3; losing every ball in play costs one and respawns a fresh ball, until
  lives reach 0 (game over). Clearing every brick on the board advances to the next level,
  carrying score and remaining lives forward.

`frontend/modules/game.ts` renders this onto a `<canvas>`, scaled to the panel's actual width
(the simulation itself always runs in the same fixed virtual board, so physics never depends on
how big the panel is drawn). Input: arrow keys / `a`/`d` to steer, mouse drag or touch to steer
directly to a position, `space` to pause. The animation loop uses real elapsed time each frame
(clamped against a multi-second gap, e.g. a backgrounded tab) and lets `stepGame`'s own
substepping absorb ordinary frame-rate variance — so play speed is the same at 30fps or 144fps.
Best score is `localStorage["adi.gamebricks.best"]`, scoped to the browser, not the backend —
there is nothing server-side to lose it with.

## Checking it works

```sh
bun test test/collision.test.ts test/levels.test.ts test/game-step.test.ts
```

37 checks with no DOM, no server: paddle bounce angle and speed conservation, wall/brick
reflection, the anti-tunnelling substep bound under a dropped-frame-sized `dt`, hand-designed
levels coming back brick-for-brick, procedural-level determinism and difficulty monotonicity, and
whole-frame scenarios through `stepGame` — brick destruction and scoring, multi-hit survival,
level-clear, lives lost and game over, and every power-up's effect.

A second, optional check covers what the logic tests structurally can't: whether the
paused/game-over overlay is actually invisible when it should be. `.gbricks__overlay` sets
`display: flex` (to centre its card), and an author stylesheet rule always outranks the UA's own
`[hidden] { display: none }` at equal specificity — so a missing `.gbricks__overlay[hidden]`
override renders the overlay (and its buttons) permanently, over the board, regardless of the
`hidden` attribute — this exact bug shipped in game-2048 v1.0.0. Neither `bun:test`'s DOM nor
happy-dom compute CSS cascade, so this needs a real browser:

```sh
bun add -d playwright && bunx playwright install chromium   # one-time, not needed to play the game
bun test test/overlay-visibility.test.ts
```

It skips (with a warning, not a failure) if Playwright isn't installed — the dashboard itself has
no dependency on it.
